items.summary: AI startup Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI staff, debuted on the stock market with a peak first-day valuation of $1.3tn. CEO Dario Amodei said the record-breaking IPO had 'strengthened' the company's resolve to 'do the right thing'. Business editor John Collingridge noted that challenges remain ahead for the global AI industry despite the debut, though he did not specify what those challenges are.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO valuation and its stated commitment to responsible development

items.summary: Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announced on Friday that Italy has granted provisional approval to Tesla's Assisted Driving System (TAD), formerly Full Self-Driving, making it the first major EU country to do so. The decision followed a technical feasibility assessment and precedes an ongoing European Union approval process; neither outcome is yet established. Salvini described the move as 'another step forward toward innovation, technology and the mobility of the future,' while Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded on X with thanks. TAD operates as a hands-off, eyes-on system requiring continuous driver supervision. Italy joins smaller EU states that already approved the system—Netherlands (April), plus Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark, and Belgium—with expansion ahead of a broader EU vote still pending.
items.title: Italy provisionally approves Tesla's TAD ahead of EU vote

items.summary: On Friday Anthropic reported that Morgan Stanley, named to stabilize its share price after the debut, exercised and thereby exhausted its full greenshoe option. The stock had fallen about 11% on Thursday from a close of $97.17 (roughly 17% above IPO) to as low as $85 before closing Friday at $86, down roughly 11.5%. Exercising the full option means Morgan Stanley can no longer use open-market purchases to cover any remaining overallotment if shares fall below the $83 IPO price; it could instead have bought additional shares directly from Anthropic at the offering price while prices were above that level on day one, which is common practice. The exercise brought aggregate gross proceeds from the IPO to roughly $93.5 billion. Market participants questioned the underwriters' timing given Thursday's technology selloff, though Morgan Stanley declined to comment. Analyst Carsten Hesse of Berenberg called it positive for Anthropic because it increases IPO proceeds but less positive for investors who lose a potential source of buying support.
items.title: Anthropic's underwriter closed its greenshoe option, removing buying support as shares fell 11%

items.summary: More than 90 separate bets on Polymarket and Kalshi relate to elements of the Jensen Huang scandal, including whether he will be arrested ($153,000 in volume), a Trump pardon (over 13,000 people betting on Kalshi), and his congressional testimony (nearly a million people betting). Traders profited by acting quickly around news breaks: user paule334 earned about $38,000 trading from Nov. 10 until the morning of Nov. 11 when The New York Times reported Huang's second affair, and Bertapotamous made nearly $100,000 on the same trade minutes after The Wall Street Journal reported he was set to resign.
items.title: Prediction-market trading on Jensen Huang story generates large profits for some traders

items.summary: OpenAI introduced a rule requiring review and approval of any gateway or router that provides third-party access to its AI models, with OpenRouter cited as the most prominent such service. The policy extends oversight beyond previously targeted gray-market 'transfer stations' in China to cover all intermediaries standing between OpenAI and end users. This move responds to US security agencies and companies including Anthropic, which have accused Chinese labs of distilling or copying American frontier models through intermediary routing that obscures the identity of the end user.
items.title: OpenAI requires approval for third-party gateways reselling its models

items.summary: On Nov. 14-15, more than 650 Indigenous protesters boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on the Tapajós River near Santarém in Pará state to demand protection for the waterway amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories. Jackson Tapajós, executive secretary of the Tupinambá Indigenous Council, told Mongabay that forest-fire smoke obscured visibility until barges approached closely. Indigenous women negotiated with armed security guards after boarding a fuel barge on Nov. 14; the guards permitted them aboard but remained alongside with guns drawn, creating tension per Tapajós's account. The river is an export artery moving soybeans and corn to Atlantic ports; according to the Ministry of Ports and Airports, cargo throughput reached 16.8 million metric tons in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024. Gilson Tupinambá, chief of the Tupinambá people, said via Amazon Watch that the river is sacred and central to their territories; its rock islands are considered home to encantados spiritual beings, and a prior decree allowing those islands' demolition for heavier ship traffic was repealed in February after a 33-day blockade of a Cargill grain terminal. None of the region's 12 Indigenous territories has full legal recognition: FUNAI had not yet begun studying claims for five (Tupinambá do Baixo Tapajós, Encantados/Kumaruara, Sarambiá, Terra Preta and Arapyun), while seven others are at varying stages with some stalled nearly two decades. Lukas Tupinambá, coordinator of the Tapajós and Arapiuns Indigenous Council (CITA), called for identifying what is missing in each case, who must advance it, and by when.
items.title: Indigenous protesters board soy and fuel barges on Brazil's Tapajós River

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India published frequently asked questions on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026. The RBI states that a resident individual exporter of services is deemed to have submitted the export declaration form when they provide payment-receipt details to their authorised dealer for crediting their account. For persons other than resident individuals, EDF submission applies only when each inward remittance exceeds ₹10 lakh or its foreign-currency equivalent; below that threshold no filing is required. The RBI also states that an authorised dealer must enter import-of-service details in the Import Data Processing and Monitoring System within five working days of receipt where the invoice or contract value exceeds ₹10 lakh, as furnished by a non-resident importer. The regulations were notified on November 02, 2026 and came into effect retrospectively from October 01, 2026; these are RBI's stated positions in its FAQs rather than independently verified outcomes.
items.title: RBI issues FAQs clarifying EDF submission rules under FEMA export/import amendment regulations

items.summary: A New York Times report, citing current and former Nvidia employees, says founder and former CEO Jensen Huang used violent language and public put-downs as a management style across nearly two decades. The accounts include reports that he told managers in front of their teams he would kill them, said an employee in their 70s everyone hoped would die, allegedly threatened to rip off an employee's head and "pee on your brain," claimed another subordinate would have both arms ripped off and beaten to death with them, threw a water bottle at an executive during anger, and wished Jay Puri, then-executive vice-president of worldwide field operations, that he get the flu, die, and end everyone's misery. Complaints reportedly date back to 2005; Michael Winston, former senior vice-president of human resources, said Huang "thinks he can get away with anything" at a two-day off-site meeting attended by around 50 employees where Huang allegedly threatened to rip out an employee's heart and stomp on it. Winston confronted Huang in November 2005, was fired that month after being told he was "not a good fit," filed complaints with California's Department of Fair Employment and Housing and drafted a lawsuit, then reached a confidential $1 million settlement before filing; Winston died earlier this year. Six current and former employees described the culture as resembling Stockholm syndrome, in which hostages bond emotionally with abusers, though Nvidia grew into an AI leader over 33 years under Huang's leadership. His daughter Madison Huang reportedly used terms such as "dead-face" for expressionless subordinates after reprimands and called employees "goldfish" when they could not remember something, per the Wall Street Journal. Despite these accounts, more than 200,000 people have signed an online petition calling for his reinstatement as CEO; Nvidia's board has not supported that idea, interim CEO Colette Kress—who was reportedly belittled by Huang during a meeting—urged employees to "move forward" at the first all-hands meeting held without him. All incidents are reported allegations attributed to unnamed sources and cited individuals.
items.title: New York Times report alleges Jensen Huang repeatedly humiliated and threatened Nvidia employees
